slides.heading: Looking up
slides.text: For thousands of years, people looked up at the night sky and wondered what was out there. In the 1950s, they finally built rockets powerful enough to find out!

slides.heading: Sputnik 1
slides.text: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first human-made satellite. It was about the size of a beach ball, and it sent 'beep-beep' radio signals from space.

slides.heading: NASA is born
slides.text: The United States created NASA, its space agency. NASA opened on October 1, 1958, to explore space for the good of everyone.

slides.heading: The first person in space
slides.text: On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space. His ship, Vostok 1, went once around Earth in 108 minutes.

slides.heading: Cosmonaut or astronaut?
slides.text: 'Cosmonaut' is the Russian word for a space traveler. Americans say 'astronaut', which comes from Greek words meaning 'star sailor'.

slides.heading: The Mercury Seven
slides.text: NASA's first program to fly people was called Project Mercury. In 1959, NASA chose seven pilots to be its very first astronauts.

image.alt: The seven Mercury astronauts in their silver spacesuits

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · The Mercury Seven astronauts

slides.heading: Freedom 7
slides.text: On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard flew the Freedom 7 capsule and became the first American in space. Let's watch NASA's film of that day!

video.credit: Video: NASA · The Day Alan Shepard Made American History

slides.heading: Your mission
slides.text: Before we can fly, we need to understand how a spaceship works. Let's explore the 8 major systems every spaceship needs!

systems.title: The 8 major systems of a spaceship
intro: Every spaceship is made of a few big systems that work together, like the parts of your body.
Scroll through the 8 systems below. Drag the 3D model to spin it and look closely at the details!
systems.doneLine: Great job! You've explored all 8 systems. Now let's use what you learned to build Freedom 7.
systems.hint: Tap each system below. Explore all 8 to continue!

items.name: Propulsion
items.subtitle: Rocket engines
items.what: Burns fuel to push the ship up. Hot gas rushes out of the bottom and the rocket moves the other way, like a balloon letting out its air.
items.where: At the bottom of the rocket. Freedom 7 rode on a Redstone rocket with one big engine.
items.fact: Rockets carry their own oxygen, so their engines still work where there is no air!

items.name: Guidance & Navigation
items.subtitle: Knowing where you're going
items.what: Spinning gyroscopes and computers keep track of which way the ship is pointing and where it is going.
items.where: Inside the rocket and the capsule. Apollo's guidance computer helped steer all the way to the Moon.
items.fact: A spinning gyroscope tries to keep pointing the same way, like a spinning top that won't fall over.

items.name: Attitude Control
items.subtitle: Small steering thrusters
items.what: Small thrusters puff out gas to turn the ship: nose up or down, left or right, or rolling around.
items.where: Around the outside of the capsule. Alan Shepard used a hand controller to fire them on Freedom 7.
items.fact: In space, 'attitude' means the direction your spaceship is facing, not how you behave!

items.name: Electrical Power
items.subtitle: Batteries, fuel cells, solar panels
items.what: Gives electricity to the radios, lights, computers and fans.
items.where: Freedom 7 used batteries. Apollo used fuel cells, and satellites and space stations use solar panels.
items.fact: Apollo's fuel cells made electricity AND drinking water for the astronauts!

items.name: Communications
items.subtitle: Radios and antennas
items.what: Radios and antennas send voices, pictures and data between the spaceship and people on Earth.
items.where: Antennas on the outside, radios inside. Giant dish antennas on Earth listen for the signals.
items.fact: Radio signals travel at the speed of light. A message from the Moon reaches Earth in just over one second!

items.name: Life Support
items.subtitle: Air, pressure and temperature
items.what: Keeps astronauts alive: it gives them oxygen, removes the carbon dioxide they breathe out, and keeps the cabin at a safe pressure and temperature.
items.where: Inside the cabin and inside the astronaut's spacesuit.
items.fact: Alan Shepard wore a pressure suit on Freedom 7, so he would stay safe even if the cabin lost its air.

items.name: Heat Shield
items.subtitle: Thermal protection
items.what: Protects the capsule when it falls back into the air super fast. It squeezes the air in front of it so hard that the air glows hotter than lava!
items.where: On the wide bottom of the capsule, which faces forward when it comes home.
items.fact: Some heat shields are made to slowly burn away on purpose, carrying the heat off with them.

items.name: Recovery & Landing
items.subtitle: Parachutes
items.what: Slows the capsule down so it can land gently.
items.where: Packed in the top of the capsule. Freedom 7 floated down under its parachute into the Atlantic Ocean.
items.fact: A small parachute opens first to steady the capsule, then the big main parachute opens.

builder.title: Build Freedom 7
intro: Here is a big box of spaceship parts from many different missions.
Freedom 7 needs exactly 6 of them. Follow the glowing arrow and tap the right parts to build it from the bottom up!
builder.doneLine: You built Freedom 7! A Redstone rocket with a Mercury capsule on top. Let's take a closer look.

parts.name: Redstone Rocket
parts.info: The Redstone rocket pushes Freedom 7 up into space. Its engine burned for about two and a half minutes.

parts.name: Retrorocket Pack
parts.info: Three small rockets strapped under the heat shield. They slow a capsule down to come home from orbit. Alan Shepard fired them as a test!

parts.name: Heat Shield
parts.info: The heat shield protects the bottom of the capsule from the heat of coming back through the air.

parts.name: Mercury Capsule
parts.info: This is Freedom 7 itself! It had room for just one astronaut. Astronauts joked that you don't climb into a Mercury capsule, you put it on.

parts.name: Parachute Section
parts.info: The top of the capsule holds the parachutes and the radio antennas.

parts.name: Launch Escape Tower
parts.info: A small rocket on a tower. If something went wrong at launch, it would pull the capsule and the astronaut away to safety.

parts.name: Solar Panels
parts.why: Freedom 7 used batteries. The whole trip lasted only about 15 minutes!

parts.name: Shuttle Wings
parts.why: Wings came 20 years later with the Space Shuttle. Freedom 7 had no wings.

parts.name: Landing Legs
parts.why: Freedom 7 splashed down in the ocean, so it didn't need legs to land.

parts.name: Rover Wheels
parts.why: Wheels are for rovers that drive on the Moon or Mars. Freedom 7 never needed to drive!

parts.name: Giant Dish Antenna
parts.why: Big dishes talk across huge distances. Freedom 7 stayed close to Earth, so small antennas were enough.

parts.name: Saturn V Rocket
parts.why: The giant Saturn V came later, for trips to the Moon. Freedom 7 only needed the Redstone.

freedom7Reveal.title: Freedom 7 is ready!
freedom7Reveal.subtitle: Mercury-Redstone 3
freedom7Reveal.line: Here it is: Freedom 7 on top of its Redstone rocket! Drag to spin it around. When you're ready, let's launch!

ascent.title: Fly to space!
intro: 3, 2, 1... Liftoff! Now YOU fly Freedom 7 up through the sky.
Steer left and right to dodge clouds, birds, balloons and meteors. Use the arrow keys, or touch and drag. Climb to 100 kilometers, where space begins!

layers.name: Troposphere
layers.fact: Troposphere: this is where all our weather happens!

layers.name: Stratosphere
layers.fact: Stratosphere: the ozone layer up here protects us from the Sun's harsh rays.

layers.name: Mesosphere
layers.fact: Mesosphere: most meteors burn up here as shooting stars!

layers.name: Thermosphere
layers.fact: Thermosphere: the air is super thin. Auroras glow up here.

ascent.spaceText: You crossed the Kármán line at 100 km. You're in SPACE!
endLines: Great flying! The real Freedom 7 kept climbing to 187 kilometers (116 miles).
Alan Shepard floated weightless for about five minutes before falling back to Earth.

slides.heading: The first photo from space
slides.text: Cameras went to space before people did! In 1946, a camera on a V-2 rocket took the first photo of Earth from space, about 105 km (65 miles) up.

slides.heading: Freedom 7's view
slides.text: During his flight, Alan Shepard looked at Earth through a periscope. He said: 'What a beautiful view!'

slides.heading: Liftoff!
slides.text: Here is the real launch of Freedom 7 from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on May 5, 1961.

image.alt: Freedom 7 lifting off on its Redstone rocket

slides.heading: Mission facts
slides.text: Flight time: 15 minutes 28 seconds. Highest point: 187 km (116 miles). Top speed: 8,262 km/h (5,134 mph).

slides.heading: Splashdown!
slides.text: Freedom 7 landed in the Atlantic Ocean. A helicopter picked up Shepard and his capsule and carried them to the ship USS Lake Champlain.

slides.heading: What happened next?
slides.text: Ten years later, Alan Shepard walked on the Moon with Apollo 14, and he even hit golf balls there!

complete.title: Chapter 1 complete!
lines: You learned the 8 systems of a spaceship.
You built Freedom 7 and flew it to space.
You saw the first pictures from space.
complete.guide: Amazing work, star sailor! Next, let's go back to 1958 and meet America's first satellite: Explorer 1.
